## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

## Refocusing our elections section

We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. ## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

Training progression of the reference pairwise reward with half of the batch being calibration training. Composite rises with training to match Opus 4.6. Audit quality surpasses Opus 4.6 while false positive calibration stays above 99%. Realism improves to matching Opus 4.6 despite not being independently optimized. Error bars are 95% CIs across seeds, with n=3 rollouts averaged per seed.

## Refocusing our elections section

We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope.

For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections.

## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

Training progression of the reference pairwise reward with half of the batch being calibration training. Composite rises with training to match Opus 4.6. Audit quality surpasses Opus 4.6 while false positive calibration stays above 99%. Realism improves to matching Opus 4.6 despite not being independently optimized. Error bars are 95% CIs across seeds, with n=3 rollouts averaged per seed.

Following the launch of our Model Hardware Standard, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. ## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

Training progression of the reference pairwise reward with half of the batch being calibration training. Composite rises with training to match Opus 4.6. Audit quality surpasses Opus 4.6 while false positive calibration stays above 99%. Realism improves to matching Opus 4.6 despite not being independently optimized. Error bars are 95% CIs across seeds, with n=3 rollouts averaged per seed.

## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

## Refocusing our elections section

We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. In this version, we’ve further sharpened our section on elections, focusing it specifically on disallowing the use of Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections (for instance, by spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, impersonating candidates or election officials, or trying to suppress turnout). We’ve renamed it Do Not Undermine Democratic Processes to reflect that scope.

For a similar reason, we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting. This prohibition covered legitimate civic work, such as nonprofits using Claude to write information for voters in other languages, or election officials sending ballot cure notices. The behaviors that motivated the original rule (like voter targeting that relies on deception or the misuse of voters’ personal data) remain prohibited under our deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and privacy sections.

## Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases

When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop” (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.

These requirements haven’t changed with the updated version of our Usage Policy. However, users have often asked us whether a given use case has these requirements, so we've rewritten our High-risk Use Case Requirements section to answer that more directly. It now lists which kinds of recommendations are covered and which are not.

Following the launch of our Model Hardware Standard, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected.

## Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations (Anthropic, 2025). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri (Fronsdal et al., 2025), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations (Kissane et al., 2026), and AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

Training progression of the reference pairwise reward with half of the batch being calibration training. Composite rises with training to match Opus 4.6. Audit quality surpasses Opus 4.6 while false positive calibration stays above 99%. Realism improves to matching Opus 4.6 despite not being independently optimized. Error bars are 95% CIs across seeds, with n=3 rollouts averaged per seed.

We’ve refined our political content restrictions in each version of our Usage Policy in order to ensure that our models can be used appropriately in democratic processes. ## Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases

When our products are used in ways that can affect someone's health, legal rights, finances, livelihood, or access to essential services, we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop” (that is, someone who has the authority to review and, if necessary, change Claude’s recommendations), and for the individual affected to be told that AI was used.

These requirements haven’t changed with the updated version of our Usage Policy. However, users have often asked us whether a given use case has these requirements, so we've rewritten our High-risk Use Case Requirements section to answer that more directly. It now lists which kinds of recommendations are covered and which are not.

Following the launch of our Model Hardware Standard, this section also adds requirements for the use of our models when they’re connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions and which might be capable of causing injury. A qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed; the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected.
